name: Freya Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a lead setter at an injection moulding plant out by the ring road. We make the plastic insides of cars: door panels, glovebox lids, the trim around the gear stick. I run a bay of six presses, the big one is 800 tonnes, and I'm the person they call when a mould starts flashing or a part comes out short. I love the moment a new tool goes in and the first good part drops onto the belt, but the heat off those barrels in July wears me right down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and who do you work alongside?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Nine years, since I was eighteen and still finishing my diploma at night. My crew is four operators and a robot that takes parts off the big press, which we call Kevin because he jams on Mondays. I'm also the union rep for our shift, so half my breaks go on people's rota problems. My partner Sami is a nurse, so between his nights and my rotating shifts we mostly talk by notes on the fridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. Every year management shows us a slideshow about smart factories, and every year the same presses are leaking the same hydraulic oil. On the union group chat I'd post something like, good, now can we talk about the broken extraction fan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's a relief. I've spent nine years learning how a mould behaves when the room is cold first thing in the morning, and I don't want that to be worth nothing. I'd keep my job, keep my rate, and keep arguing about the same things I argue about now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly nothing new, which is how I like it. I'd keep putting a few hundred a month into savings like I already do, and keep pushing the safety committee about the fan. If they bring in some AI scheduling program I'd let the planners deal with it, because I don't touch that stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit smug. Like when a storm warning comes and it just rains a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at work that would change even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the camera system they put on line three last spring. It checks parts for scratches, and it does catch things, but it also throws out good parts and someone has to dig them out of the scrap bin. A machine that's wrong half the time still needs a person standing next to it, and that's been my job security.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never use AI tools. Has anyone pushed you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My shift manager Dev keeps telling me to use some app to write my handover notes. I write them on paper, in capitals, and pin them on the board, and nobody has ever misread one. I'm not against technology, I run machines worth more than my flat, but I don't want a chatbot between me and my crew.

S0.say: I'd tell everyone I said so all along, because the smart factory slides never changed the leaking presses. On the union chat I'd turn it back to real problems like the broken extraction fan.
S0.think: I'm quietly relieved, because nine years of knowing how a mould behaves would still be worth something. I'd keep my job, my rate and my usual fights.
S0.do: Keeps working as now and keeps saving a few hundred a month as she already does. Keeps pushing the safety committee on the extraction fan and leaves any AI scheduling tools to the planners.
S0.feel: Calm and a little smug, like a storm warning that turns into light rain.
S0.quote: A machine that's wrong half the time still needs a person standing next to it, and that's been my job security.
S0.fieldNote: Freya's security is built on knowing machines that misbehave, so a plateau confirms her worldview. She separates trusting machinery from trusting software, and she is proud of her paper handover notes. Her union role colours everything; she turns even good news into a workplace demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is exactly why we need the union at the table before anything gets installed. I'd want it in writing that nobody gets laid off because of a new system, only moved and trained. Online I'd probably share articles about workers getting a say over technology, that's my kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it worries me more than I'd say on the shop floor. The robot on the big press already does what two operators did when I started. If that spreads to the other five presses, my bay goes from four operators to maybe one, and I'd be the one picking who stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd get the union to open talks about a technology agreement, before the company buys anything. I'd keep saving, maybe push it up to six hundred a month, because Sami and I want a deposit on a house in a few years. I wouldn't jump to another plant, there are plenty around here, but they'd all be doing the same thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared yet, but I'd notice it every time a supplier rep walked through with a tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be the one picking who stays. Who comes to mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta, straight away. She's been on the presses twenty years, she's brilliant with her hands, but she can't read the new screens without her glasses and she won't ask for help. If they cut my bay down, I'd have to look Marta in the eye at the break table, and I've known her since I was eighteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the new systems yourself, if that kept you in the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they made it part of the job and trained us on paid time, yes, I'd do it. I just wouldn't go home and play with it on my phone. I'd rather be the person who knows the hydraulics better than anyone than the person who's good at the software.

S1.say: I'd say this is why the union has to be at the table before any new system is installed. I'd want written promises that people get moved and trained, not laid off.
S1.think: Privately I'm more worried than I'd admit, because one robot already does the work of two operators. If it spreads across my presses, my crew shrinks and I end up choosing who stays.
S1.do: Pushes the union to open talks on a technology agreement before the company buys new systems. Raises her savings to about six hundred a month toward a house deposit with Sami and stays at her plant rather than moving.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a background worry that comes back every time a supplier rep walks through with a tablet.
S1.quote: If they cut my bay down, I'd have to look Marta in the eye at the break table, and I've known her since I was eighteen.
S1.fieldNote: The thought that hurts her is choosing between colleagues, not losing her own job. She will learn new systems only on paid time, which says a lot about how she sees the boundary between work and life. Her answer is collective first, personal second.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be furious, and I'd say so. I'd be telling everyone this is the biggest grab of all time, a handful of companies owning the machines that do everybody's work. Online I'd be sharing every petition for a robot tax and a basic income, and I'd be at every meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't know what I am in two years. I'm 27, I've got a diploma in plastics processing and nine years on presses, and that's it. If a robot can set a mould and fix a flashing part, then everything I'm good at is gone, and I've never learned anything else because I never wanted to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything that isn't rent and food, straight away, and keep the savings untouched. We'd put the house plan on ice. I'd throw myself into the union and the local campaign for a robot tax, because that's the only lever I can see that's the size of the problem. I wouldn't know what to retrain for, because two years isn't enough to retrain for anything a robot couldn't also do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, mostly. Like the floor tilting and nothing to hold on to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the savings actually buy you in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe eighteen months if we're careful, because Sami would still be earning, at least at first. But it's not really the money, it's that I'd be sitting at home at 28 with nothing to get up for. I've been the one people call when a press breaks down. In two years, nobody's calling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you hold responsible, if it goes like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies that own it, and the governments that let them race ahead without a plan. Not the engineers, not the robot, the people who decided profit gets there first and workers get sorted out later. I'd want them to pay for what comes after, properly, through tax.

S2.say: I'd call it the biggest grab of all time, with a few companies owning the machines that do everyone's work. I'd share every petition for a robot tax and a basic income and turn up to every meeting.
S2.think: Privately I don't know who I am in two years, because everything I'm good at would be gone. I'm 27 with one trade and I never learned anything else because I never wanted to.
S2.do: Cuts spending to rent and food straight away, freezes the house plan and leaves savings untouched. Throws herself into union work and the local robot tax campaign rather than retraining, since she cannot see a trade a robot couldn't also do.
S2.feel: Sick, like the floor tilting with nothing to hold on to.
S2.quote: I've been the one people call when a press breaks down. In two years, nobody's calling.
S2.fieldNote: Her resistance to change leaves her with no plan B, and she knows it. The money would last, but she fears losing purpose more than losing income. She aims her anger at owners and governments, not at the technology, and puts all her energy into collective answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much what I'd say with the fast one, but I'd have more time to get organised about it. I'd be telling people at work that five years is enough time to win something if we start now. I'd want the union pushing for job guarantees and a share of what the robots earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years means I'd have to do something I don't want to do, which is change. I'd be 32 when it arrives, and that's young enough that nobody's going to feel sorry for me. I'd still be grieving the work, but I couldn't pretend I had no time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving hard and keep the house plan on hold until I could see where things were heading. I'd go all in on the union, maybe stand for a regional role. And I suppose I'd look at the nursing access course Sami keeps going on about, because people looking after sick people feels like the last thing anyone wants a robot doing, but I'd drag my feet on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less of a punch than two years, more of a weight I'd carry around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd drag your feet. What would stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being a beginner again, at 30, around a lot of 19-year-olds. I'm the best setter in the building. I don't want to be the slowest person in a classroom. I know that's pride, but it's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Sami say about you following him into nursing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd laugh and then he'd tell me about the robot trolleys they already have on his ward that deliver meds. That's the thing, he's not sure nursing is safe either. So I'd be giving up something I'm great at for something that might also go.

S3.say: I'd tell people at work that five years is enough to win something if we start organising now. I'd want the union pushing for job guarantees and a share of what the robots earn.
S3.think: Privately, five years means I'd have to change, which I really don't want. I'd be 32 when it arrives, too young for anyone to feel sorry for me.
S3.do: Keeps saving hard and leaves the house plan on hold while she sees where things go. Goes deeper into the union, possibly standing for a regional role, and reluctantly looks into a nursing access course.
S3.feel: Anxious, less of a punch than the two-year version and more of a weight she would carry around.
S3.quote: I'm the best setter in the building. I don't want to be the slowest person in a classroom.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time turns her problem from shock into a choice she doesn't want to make. Pride is the real block to retraining, and she says so herself. Even the escape route she considers, nursing, already looks less safe to her through Sami's stories about robot trolleys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if politicians actually use it, and a disaster if they waste it like they waste everything else. I'd be pushing for the plant to commit to retraining every worker on paid time, starting now. I'd post about it, but I'd be careful not to sound like the world is ending, because people tune that out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd be 37, and I could still have a whole second career after it. That's not nothing. But honestly I'd probably spend the first few years telling myself it might not happen, because that's what I'm like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first few years, I'd keep working the presses and keep saving, and Sami and I would probably still buy the house, just a smaller one so the payments are safe on one wage. I'd use the union to get a paid training scheme at the plant. Somewhere around year five, if it was clearly coming, I'd start a proper course, maybe nursing, maybe something in care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared. It feels like something far down the road that I'd keep glancing at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell yourself it might not happen. Is that a plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. It's a hope wearing a hard hat. I'd still save, and I'd still push the union, so I'm not doing nothing, but the personal stuff I'd put off as long as I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would ten years change the conversations with your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want us to talk about it at the break table every month, not once when the layoff letters come. Marta would be retired by then, lucky her. The young lads would be the ones I'd worry about, because they think the robot on the big press is funny.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift if politicians use it and a disaster if they waste it. I'd push the plant to commit to paid retraining for every worker, without sounding like the world is ending.
S4.think: I'd be 37, young enough for a whole second career, which matters. But I'd probably spend the first few years telling myself it might not happen.
S4.do: Keeps running the presses and saving, and buys a smaller house with Sami that one wage could cover. Uses the union to win a paid training scheme and starts a proper course, likely in nursing or care, around year five if it is clearly coming.
S4.feel: Uneasy more than scared, like something far down the road she keeps glancing at.
S4.quote: It's a hope wearing a hard hat.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets her keep her trade for now and plan the change on her own slow timetable. She admitted with humour that her wait-and-see stance is a hope rather than a plan. Her worry shifts from Marta to the young operators who still laugh at the robot.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, by miles. Two years is no time for someone like me, who's slow to change on purpose. I'd need someone to pay me while I figure out who I am without a press to fix. A proper wage while I retrain, paid for by the companies that own the robots, would actually help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd miss it, and I would. People think factory work is just standing there, but there's a craft to it, and I'm good at it. Nobody's going to make a documentary about the last great injection moulding setter.

headlineQuote: I'd need someone to pay me while I figure out who I am without a press to fix.
portrait: Freya Haddad, 27, is the lead setter and union rep on her shift at an injection moulding plant that makes car interior parts. She trusts machines she can fix with her hands but keeps away from AI tools, writing her handover notes on paper. A plateau leaves her calm and a little smug, steady disruption makes her worry about choosing which colleague goes, and fast AGI leaves her alarmed and without a plan B. With more warning she slowly accepts she'd have to retrain, likely towards nursing or care, but admits she would put it off as long as she could. She blames owners and governments rather than the technology, and wants the robots' owners to pay for workers' transition.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because two years is no time for someone who is slow to change on purpose.
whatWouldHelp: A proper wage while she retrains, paid for by the companies that own the robots.
